text: Two papers analyse amenable (treatable) mortality. The first compares Hungary, Czechoslovakia, Poland and East Germany with West Germany, England and Wales, the US and Canada (1950s–1987). All-cause mortality trends diverged around 1970: Western rates fell steadily while Eastern ones stagnated. At ages 0–64, amenable mortality declined more slowly in Eastern Europe, and non-amenable mortality rose from the late 1960s against substantial Western declines—the principal reason for Eastern Europe's stalled improvement. Priorities should be healthier lifestyles, environment and better health services. Scholz compares Lithuania, Hungary and Romania with West Germany (1980/81–1988 and 1992–1997): West German temporary life expectancy (e0–75) rose 2.7 years (men) and 1.6 (women); Hungarian women gained 1.3; Romanian men lost 1.3. Falling infant mortality, largely amenable, contributed substantially.
